findings.commentary: The functions this advisory is about are still in the kotlin-stdlib the 24 series resolve, and nothing calls them. The advisory is createTempDir and createTempFile in kotlin.io creating files a local user can read. Kotlin 1.4.21 deprecated them and Kotlin 2.1.0 made them an error, which is why the advisory database says before 1.4.21 and NVD says before 2.1.0. The 24 series resolve 1.9.25, where they still exist, and no library on the classpath calls them. The 25 series resolve 2.3.21, outside both ranges.
findings.impact: None. Nothing in the application calls the two deprecated functions.

findings.commentary: CVE-2021-3163 is a Quill advisory, and DOMPurify is not Quill. The production build of Vaadin 24.9 and 24.10 puts DOMPurify, which Markdown uses, and Quill, which Rich Text Editor bundles, into the same generated JavaScript file. Your scanner names that file DOMPurify from its licence header and then matches the Quill CPE against it. The Quill in that file is a separate finding with its own verdict, npm-quill-2021-3163. The flaw is real in the Quill that Rich Text Editor bundles, and Vaadin keeps the payload away from it. Every 24 release carries Quill 1.3.6, inside the advisory, and that Quill runs an IMG event handler when it is handed raw HTML. RichTextEditor cleans every value with jsoup in both directions, on what a browser sends and on what setValue shows, and no on* attribute survives. You are exposed only if your code puts HTML into the editor another way: callJsFunction or executeJs with dangerouslySetHtmlValue, or the vaadin-rich-text-editor element used from client code with HTML someone else wrote.
findings.fix_expected: None upstream: GHSA-4943-9vgg-gr5r says no patch exists and no further Quill 1 releases are planned.
findings.impact: None from DOMPurify, which this advisory does not describe. The Quill code in the same file is covered by the verdict npm-quill-2021-3163. None through RichTextEditor.setValue or the editor itself, which clean the HTML. HTML that reaches the editor in the browser without that cleaning can run script in the browser of whoever views it.

findings.commentary: One method of this library overflows the stack on a very long argument, and nothing in Vaadin calls it. ClassUtils.getClass recurses on a class name, so a name thousands of characters long throws a StackOverflowError. Its only callers on the classpath are in Commons Text and Commons Configuration: their ${const:...} lookups and the bean declarations of Commons Configuration. You reach them only by feeding that interpolation, or such a configuration, text somebody else wrote. Spring Boot 3.5 picks the version, 3.17.0, and Vaadin does not.
findings.fix_expected: No Spring Boot 3.5 release carries it: the newest, 3.5.16, pins 3.17.0.
findings.impact: None unless the application runs Commons Text or Commons Configuration interpolation over untrusted input. There a long class name stops the thread with an Error that most code does not catch.

packages.workaround: With spring-boot-starter-parent, set <commons-lang3.version>3.18.0</commons-lang3.version> in the properties of your pom. Without that parent, declare org.apache.commons:commons-lang3 3.18.0 in your dependencyManagement. Measured on 2026-10-24 on Spring Boot 3.5.16: the property moves 24.9.24 and 24.10.12 from 3.17.0 to 3.18.0. That measures resolution, not compatibility.

findings.commentary: Your scanner has matched the product and not the module. The CPE it used, eclipse:vert.x, names the whole project, and Eclipse published a batch of advisories on the same day that all read "in Eclipse Vert.x versions [4.0.0, 4.5.34]", so every one of them lands on every Vert.x jar your application resolves. An application with Control Center resolves two, vertx-core and vertx-web-client, and each of these advisories is filed against a module it does not resolve: vertx-web, vertx-json-schema, vertx-sql-client, vertx-mqtt, vertx-redis-client, vertx-mail-client and vertx-grpc. The advisories are real where they belong and none of those modules is here. The thirteenth advisory of that batch, CVE-2026-102467, does name vertx-core and is answered on its own. findings.commentary: Real in vertx-core 4.5.34, and the path that carries it is never opened. The advisory needs a compressed WebSocket frame, and compression is negotiated: Vert.x 4.5.34 offers neither per message nor per frame compression by default, and the fabric8 Kubernetes client that owns this connection never turns either on, so no frame is ever decompressed. Vert.x is here only with Control Center, as the HTTP client fabric8 uses to reach your cluster's Kubernetes API server, not as a server facing your users. findings.commentary: Nothing you deploy runs vite: Vaadin names it as a development dependency, a production build runs it once to make the bundle, and the archive carries the bundle. All five are about the development server. Three are in launch-editor, which that server uses to open a file in your editor from the error overlay; one is script execution through custom middleware, and one serves files outside server.fs.allow on a server exposed to the network. Each needs that server running plus the condition its advisory states.

findings.commentary: The DOMPurify your scanner found is inside the JavaScript file that the Vaadin 24.9 and 24.10 build produces, not in node_modules. In that file the only code that calls DOMPurify is the Markdown component, which passes one option, CUSTOM_ELEMENT_HANDLING, and registers no hook. These three advisories need options Vaadin never sets: SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES with a mode that returns DOM, IN_PLACE with a hook of your own that removes nodes, or PARSER_MEDIA_TYPE set to application/xhtml+xml. Only code of your own can create those conditions. The same library also reaches your build through node_modules, and that copy is answered by npm-dompurify-markdown-24-9-2026-10-23. These three are DOMPurify advisories, and Quill is not DOMPurify. The production build of Vaadin 24.9 and 24.10 puts Quill, which Rich Text Editor bundles, and DOMPurify, which Markdown uses, into the same generated JavaScript file. Your scanner names that file Quill and gives it the DOMPurify advisories that belong to the other library in it. The DOMPurify in that file has its own verdict, javascript-dompurify-markdown-24-9. DOMPurify reaches a Vaadin 24.9 or 24.10 application through @vaadin/markdown, the only caller in the frontend Vaadin ships, which sanitises a string with one option, CUSTOM_ELEMENT_HANDLING, and registers no hook. These three need options Vaadin never sets: SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES with a DOM returning mode, IN_PLACE with a hook of your own that removes nodes, or PARSER_MEDIA_TYPE set to application/xhtml+xml. Only your own code can create those conditions.
findings.fix_expected: Upstream 3.4.17 fixes all three. Your build moves to it when a Vaadin release moves the dompurify pin in @vaadin/bundles, as described in npm-dompurify-markdown-24-9-2026-10-23. Upstream 3.4.17 clears all three. @vaadin/bundles 24.9.20 and 24.10.8 declare dompurify 3.4.16 exactly as a peer dependency, and the scans of 24.9.25 and 24.10.13 resolve 3.4.16, so it moves when a Vaadin release moves that pin.
findings.impact: None through the Markdown component. If your own code calls DOMPurify with those options, it is exposed as each advisory describes. None from Quill, which these advisories do not describe. The DOMPurify code in the same file is covered by the verdict javascript-dompurify-markdown-24-9. None through the Markdown component. Code of your own that calls DOMPurify with those options is exposed as each advisory describes.

findings.commentary: The copy that matters is not the one your scanner found. OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application through Observability Kit, and Observability Kit 3 works through a Java agent that carries its own OpenTelemetry inside it. That agent extracts the W3C trace context of every incoming request with the tracestate parser this advisory describes: a long run of spaces or tabs costs CPU that grows with the square of its length. Agents up to 3.2.1 carry it, because the parser comes from the upstream Java agent the kit is built on rather than from the OpenTelemetry version it declares; the 3.2.2 agent, published on 2026-11-11, carries the rewritten parser, so what remains exposed is an agent older than that. The opentelemetry-api jar your scanner reports is a different copy, and nothing in a Vaadin application passes it an incoming header unless your own code does. Without Observability Kit that jar arrives only through TestBench, which parses no incoming header.
findings.fix_expected: The observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 on Maven Central, published on 2026-11-11, built on the upstream Java agent 2.33.1, whose shaded parser scans the header instead of compiling a pattern for it.
findings.impact: None unless the application runs an Observability Kit agent older than 3.2.2, or code of its own extracts trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header, a denial of service and not a way in.

packages.workaround: Update the agent to observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 from Maven Central; it is the jar the JVM is started with, so no application rebuild is involved. Until then, cap or remove the tracestate header at your proxy or load balancer before requests reach the application, or start the agent with -Dotel.propagators=none if you do not need trace context from upstream callers. findings.commentary: The code is there: minimatch 9.0.9 and 10.2.6 carry the pattern optimiser the advisory describes, and glob calls it with optimizationLevel 2. What it needs is an attacker who chooses the glob pattern, and in a Vaadin build nobody outside the project does. minimatch runs only on the build machine, under glob and workbox-build, and is not in the bundle the browser loads. The patterns it is handed are fixed by Vaadin, **/* for the service worker and *.css for the theme, or written by the developer in the assets section of their own theme.json. 5.1.9, the other copy on these lines, predates the optimiser.
findings.impact: None unless your own build code passes a glob pattern that someone outside your team can choose to glob or minimatch. There, a crafted pattern makes the build spend excessive CPU and memory.

findings.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
findings.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.

findings.commentary: Four Spring Security advisories filed under the product name vmware:spring_security, about code in other Spring Security jars. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong. CVE-2026-59276, which is about this jar, has its own verdict. Five Spring Security advisories landed on this jar because the scanner matched the product name vmware:spring_security, which every artifact of the project carries. None of the five is about this one: DPoP proof replay, WebAuthn user verification, the AES encryptor, the embedded UnboundID LDAP server and a set of non constant time comparisons are all in other Spring Security jars. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong.

findings.commentary: Seventeen advisories that are real at the netty every Vaadin 24 line resolves today, 4.1.115.Final to 4.1.135.Final, each on its own artifact: netty-codec, codec-dns, codec-haproxy, codec-http2, codec-redis, codec-stomp, codec-xml, handler, handler-ssl-ocsp and transport-sctp. A production Vaadin application never runs it: Tomcat serves your requests, and netty is there because Copilot, a development mode tool, declares it. Nothing outside netty refers to the stomp, xml, redis, sctp or OCSP code at all. The rest runs only when your own code uses reactor-netty (WebClient, WebFlux), or on 24.9 and 24.10 when Control Center runs on Kubernetes, whose client reaches your API server through Vert.x on netty. Otherwise nothing calls it; if one applies, set the property below.
findings.fix_expected: Spring Boot decides this version, not Vaadin. No free Spring Boot release a Vaadin 24 line declares pins a fixed netty: 3.2.12, 3.4.13 and 3.5.16, the newest of their lines on 2026-10-24, pin 4.1.115.Final, 4.1.130.Final and 4.1.135.Final. It arrives when Spring Boot raises netty.version; until then, the property.
findings.impact: None for a production application without Control Center that makes no reactor-netty calls of its own. Otherwise the code handles traffic with the servers your own client calls, or with your Kubernetes API server.

Measured on 2026-10-24 on 24.4.26, 24.7.17, 24.9.24 and 24.10.12: it moves every io.netty artifact to 4.1.139.Final, which osv.dev lists clean. That measures resolution, not compatibility, so run your tests. If your pom only imports spring-boot-dependencies, the property does nothing and you manage the io.netty artifacts in your own dependencyManagement instead, which was not measured here.

packages.commentary: Seventeen advisories that are real at the netty every Vaadin 24 line resolves today, 4.1.115.Final to 4.1.135.Final, each on its own artifact: netty-codec, codec-dns, codec-haproxy, codec-http2, codec-redis, codec-stomp, codec-xml, handler, handler-ssl-ocsp and transport-sctp. A production Vaadin application never runs it: Tomcat serves your requests, and netty is there because Copilot, a development mode tool, declares it. Nothing outside netty refers to the stomp, xml, redis, sctp or OCSP code at all. The rest runs only when your own code uses reactor-netty (WebClient, WebFlux), or on 24.9 and 24.10 when Control Center runs on Kubernetes, whose client reaches your API server through Vert.x on netty. Otherwise nothing calls it; if one applies, set the property below.
packages.fix_expected: Spring Boot decides this version, not Vaadin. No free Spring Boot release a Vaadin 24 line declares pins a fixed netty: 3.2.12, 3.4.13 and 3.5.16, the newest of their lines on 2026-10-24, pin 4.1.115.Final, 4.1.130.Final and 4.1.135.Final. It arrives when Spring Boot raises netty.version; until then, the property.

findings.commentary: OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application only through Observability Kit; TestBench brings the same jar at test scope. An oversized W3C baggage header makes the parser allocate without a bound, and baggage propagation is on by default. Which release decides the version depends on the shape of the application. With Spring Boot its dependency management pins 1.31.0 on 24.4, 1.43.0 on 24.7 and 1.49.0 on 24.9 and 24.10, all affected. Without Spring Boot the version is the one the Observability Kit the platform pins carries: 1.23.0 on 24.4 through kit 3.0.0 and 1.44.1 on 24.7 through kit 3.1.0, both affected, while 24.9 and 24.10 pin kit 3.2.1, which carries 1.62.0, so that shape is already past it. The 25 series resolve 1.62.0, which is fixed.
findings.fix_expected: With Spring Boot, on 24.4 and 24.7 none from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends those lines at 3.2.12 and 3.4.13, which pin 1.31.0 and 1.43.0, and later releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. On 24.9 and 24.10 a Spring Boot 3.5 patch pinning 1.62.0, which does not exist yet: 3.5.16, the newest open one, pins 1.49.0. Without Spring Boot, 24.9 and 24.10 already resolve 1.62.0 through Observability Kit 3.2.1 and need nothing, and on 24.4 and 24.7 the exit is an Observability Kit release built for those lines, a 3.1.1 from the 3.1.0 tag carrying a fixed OpenTelemetry, and a platform release pinning it on both branches. Kit 3.2.1 and later cannot be that release: they fail at startup on any Flow before 24.9.
findings.impact: None unless a Vaadin 24 application declares observability-kit-starter and whoever can send a baggage header can reach it. There it is a denial of service through memory and CPU, not a way in.

packages.impact: None unless a Vaadin 24 application declares observability-kit-starter and whoever can send a baggage header can reach it. There it is a denial of service through memory and CPU, not a way in.
packages.workaround: With Spring Boot, set <opentelemetry.version>1.62.0</opentelemetry.version> in your pom; take it out once your Spring Boot pins 1.62.0 or later. Without Spring Boot that property moves nothing, because only Spring Boot's dependency management reads it: import io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-bom 1.62.0 in dependencyManagement. Do not declare observability-kit-starter 3.2.1 yourself on 24.4 or 24.7: since 3.2.0 its license listener extends a Flow class that first ships in flow-server 24.9, the listener is a registered service init listener, and the application fails at startup with NoClassDefFoundError. In every case resolution was measured, not compatibility with Observability Kit. If you do not use baggage, otel.propagators=tracecontext drops the baggage propagator instead. These moves change the jar your application resolves and not the copy inside the Observability Kit agent, which carries its own: the 3.2.1 and 4.1.2 agents carry OpenTelemetry 1.62.0 and 1.65.0, both past this one, and the 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 agents carry 1.23.0 and 1.44.1, which are not.

findings.commentary: Four Spring Security advisories filed under the product name vmware:spring_security, about code in other Spring Security jars. DPoP proof replay is in spring-security-oauth2-jose, the WebAuthn bypass in spring-security-web, the AES encryptor in spring-security-crypto, and the embedded UnboundID LDAP server in spring-security-ldap, which a Vaadin application does not resolve. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong. CVE-2026-59276, which is about this jar, has its own verdict. Five Spring Security advisories landed on this jar because the scanner matched the product name vmware:spring_security, which every artifact of the project carries. None of the five is about this one: DPoP proof replay, WebAuthn user verification, the AES encryptor, the embedded UnboundID LDAP server and a set of non constant time comparisons are all in other Spring Security jars. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong.
findings.impact: None through this coordinate.

findings.commentary: The advisory is about a server your application does not start. Pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests make the Reactor Netty HTTP server hold on to memory, and a Vaadin application is served by the embedded Tomcat its Spring Boot starts, not by Reactor Netty. The library is here because Copilot, the development mode tool, uses it as an HTTP client, and a client does not accept pipelined requests from anybody. Outside Reactor Netty, only Spring's reactive web server support refers to the server class, and Spring Boot builds that server only for a reactive application, which a Vaadin application is not.
findings.impact: None. No Reactor Netty server is ever created, so nothing listens for the requests the advisory describes.

findings.commentary: Two open redirects that need a component only your own configuration registers. Your scanner reports them on spring-core; CVE-2026-47883 is about UrlHandlerFilter in spring-web and CVE-2026-47887 about UrlFilenameViewController in spring-webmvc. Nothing on a Vaadin 24 classpath refers to either class except the class itself. CVE-2026-47883 starts at 6.2.0, so 24.4 is below it; 24.7 and later are in range, as every 24 series is for CVE-2026-47887.
findings.fix_expected: Fixed on Maven Central only in Spring Framework 7.0.9, which needs Spring Boot 4 and so Vaadin 25. The 6.2 fix, 6.2.20, is published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, where the 2026-11-19 Spring cycle added 6.2.21; Maven Central still ends 6.2 at 6.2.19 and answers 404 for both, read on 2026-11-20.
findings.impact: None unless the application registers UrlHandlerFilter with very broad patterns, or maps UrlFilenameViewController with an end of path pattern and no prefix. There a crafted link redirects to another site.

findings.commentary: Your scanner matched the product, not the artifact: cpe vmware:spring_framework puts every Spring Framework advisory on spring-core. None of these nine is about spring-core. CVE-2026-47884 and CVE-2026-47890 are about spring-webmvc and are answered on that coordinate. The other seven are about Spring WebFlux, RSocket and the FreeMarker template loader, and spring-webflux, spring-messaging and spring-context-support are not resolved by a Vaadin 24.9 or 24.10 application. Two critical Spring MVC advisories about features a Vaadin application does not use. CVE-2026-47884 needs your application to render through XsltView under a /** mapping that renders a view without naming it, which turns into server side request forgery and then remote code execution. CVE-2026-47890 needs Server Sent Events returning view fragments, and starts at 6.2.0. Nothing on a Vaadin classpath refers to XsltView, SseEmitter or FragmentsRendering except spring-webmvc itself, and Vaadin pushes through Atmosphere. If you have MVC controllers of either shape, read these on your own code, where they are critical.
findings.fix_expected: Fixed publicly only in Spring Framework 7.0.9, which needs Spring Boot 4 and so Vaadin 25. spring.io marks 6.2.20 and 6.1.29 Enterprise Support Only.
findings.impact: None through spring-core. If you add Spring WebFlux, RSocket or FreeMarker yourself, read these on that code. None from Vaadin. For an application that renders XsltView under a /** mapping, CVE-2026-47884 is remote code execution: the verdict is that Vaadin does not create the condition, not that the condition is harmless.

findings.commentary: About a path nothing in a Vaadin application takes. When a MapMessage holds NaN or an infinity, MapMessage.asJson emits that bare token and the result is not valid JSON. The advisory names two conditions: a layout that calls asJson, such as the message resolver of JsonTemplateLayout, and a non finite number logged through a MapMessage. Spring Boot logs through Logback, and neither log4j-core nor JsonTemplateLayout is on the classpath of any 24 series. You would reach this only by switching to spring-boot-starter-log4j2, configuring that layout and logging a MapMessage yourself.
findings.fix_expected: None published: Spring Boot 3.2.12, 3.4.13 and 3.5.16, the newest of the lines these series use, pin Log4j 2.21.1, 2.24.3 and 2.24.3.
findings.impact: None as a Vaadin application is put together. With Log4j 2 as the backend and the JSON template layout, a log entry carrying NaN or Infinity becomes a document a conformant parser refuses, which breaks log collection rather than the application.

findings.commentary: Your scanner has matched the wrong product. The CPE it used, opentelemetry:opentelemetry, names the project rather than a package and carries the platform each record is about: CVE-2026-54285 is an advisory of opentelemetry-js on node.js, and the other four are advisories of the Go implementation. None is about a Java artifact, but the Java libraries share the product name, so each lands on every io.opentelemetry jar your application resolves. The range is open because the claim is about which implementation the records name, which no Java version changes. Nothing to upgrade for these. The package is there and the vulnerable code is not reached. The advisory is about W3CBaggagePropagator.extract, which parses baggage headers arriving from somewhere else. findings.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
findings.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.

findings.commentary: Real on 24.9 and 24.10. Their releases declare Spring Boot 3.5.5 to 3.5.16, which pin Tomcat 10.1.44 to 10.1.55, and NVD puts all eight inside ranges that end at 10.1.55 or 10.1.56. findings.commentary: Four Spring Security advisories filed under the product name vmware:spring_security, about code in other Spring Security jars. DPoP proof replay is in spring-security-oauth2-jose, the WebAuthn bypass in spring-security-web, the AES encryptor in spring-security-crypto, and the embedded UnboundID LDAP server in spring-security-ldap, which a Vaadin application does not resolve. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong. CVE-2026-59276, which is about this jar, has its own verdict. Five Spring Security advisories landed on this jar because the scanner matched the product name vmware:spring_security, which every artifact of the project carries. None of the five is about this one: DPoP proof replay, WebAuthn user verification, the AES encryptor, the embedded UnboundID LDAP server and a set of non constant time comparisons are all in other Spring Security jars. The versions are in range, 6.4.13 on 24.7 and 6.5 on 24.9 and 24.10; the coordinate is what is wrong.
findings.impact: None through this coordinate.

findings.commentary: This one is really about this jar, and about a class nothing creates for you. Of the five components the advisory names as comparing secrets with String.equals, the one in spring-security-core is KeyBasedPersistenceTokenService. Spring Security does not register it, Spring Boot does not auto configure it and no Vaadin artifact mentions it, on 24.7 as on 24.9 and 24.10. Search your sources for KeyBasedPersistenceTokenService; if it is not there, nothing in this jar is exposed by this advisory. findings.commentary: Real on every 24 series, and on 24.9 and 24.10 the releases that fix six of them are only Broadcom's commercial ones. Your scanner reports these on spring-core, but they are about spring-core, spring-expression, spring-beans, spring-web and spring-webmvc, all in your application, and nothing else reports them. CVE-2026-41848 is fixed in 6.2.19. The other six are in range through 6.2.19, the last 6.2 on Maven Central, and fixed publicly only in Spring Framework 7.0.9, which needs Spring Boot 4 and so Vaadin 25.
findings.fix_expected: The releases that fix these, spring-core 6.1.29 and 6.2.20, are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, and the 2026-11-19 Spring cycle moved that stream on to 6.1.30, 6.2.21 and Spring Boot 3.5.18: Maven Central still ends the free lines at 6.1.21, 6.2.19 and Spring Boot 3.5.16 and answers 404 for all three of the newer ones, read on 2026-11-20.

findings.commentary: This needs the writable /actuator/env endpoint, which is off unless you switch it on. Spring Cloud lets a POST to /actuator/env set any property, with no allow list of keys. spring-cloud-commons and spring-cloud-context arrive only with Control Center, and Control Center also brings Spring Boot Actuator, so the endpoint code is on your classpath. It is registered only when you set management.endpoint.env.post.enabled and expose the env endpoint over HTTP; Spring Boot exposes only health by default, and Control Center sets neither property.
findings.fix_expected: The advisory fixes the 4.3 line in 4.3.4, which is published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support and not on Maven Central, whose 4.3 metadata ended at 4.3.3 when read on 2026-10-24.
findings.impact: None unless the application sets management.endpoint.env.post.enabled=true and exposes the env endpoint over HTTP. Where both are true, whoever reaches the endpoint sets any property they like.

findings.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
findings.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.

findings.commentary: Seventeen advisories that are real at the netty every Vaadin 24 line resolves today, 4.1.115.Final to 4.1.135.Final, each on its own artifact: netty-codec, codec-dns, codec-haproxy, codec-http2, codec-redis, codec-stomp, codec-xml, handler, handler-ssl-ocsp and transport-sctp. A production Vaadin application never runs it: Tomcat serves your requests, and netty is there because Copilot, a development mode tool, declares it. Nothing outside netty refers to the stomp, xml, redis, sctp or OCSP code at all. The rest runs only when your own code uses reactor-netty (WebClient, WebFlux), or on 24.9 and 24.10 when Control Center runs on Kubernetes, whose client reaches your API server through Vert.x on netty. Otherwise nothing calls it; if one applies, set the property below.

findings.commentary: Real on 24.9 and 24.10. Their releases declare Spring Boot 3.5.5 to 3.5.16, which pin Tomcat 10.1.44 to 10.1.55, and NVD puts all ten inside ranges ending at 10.1.57; CVE-2026-65637 applies only from 10.1.53, which is 24.9.14 and 24.10.1 onwards. Spring Boot 3.5.16, the newest 3.5 on Maven Central, still pins 10.1.55, so nothing upstream fixes it yet. Tomcat names 10.1.58 as the fix, which Maven Central never published: use 10.1.62.
findings.fix_expected: A Spring Boot 3.5 patch that pins Tomcat 10.1.59 or later, and then a 24.9 or 24.10 release that declares it. Neither is published as of 2026-11-20, when Maven Central still ends Spring Boot 3.5 at 3.5.16 and answers 404 for the 3.5.18 of the 2026-11-19 Spring cycle, which is commercial only.
findings.impact: Every Vaadin 24.9 and 24.10 application on the embedded Tomcat. Most of the ten need a Tomcat feature a Spring Boot application does not configure by default (FORM or DIGEST authentication, DataSourceRealm, security-role-ref, the rewrite valve, unix domain sockets); CVE-2026-73180 is about WebSocket sessions outliving the HTTP session, and Vaadin push uses WebSocket.

findings.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
findings.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.

findings.commentary: Seventeen advisories that are real at the netty every Vaadin 24 line resolves today, 4.1.115.Final to 4.1.135.Final, each on its own artifact: netty-codec, codec-dns, codec-haproxy, codec-http2, codec-redis, codec-stomp, codec-xml, handler, handler-ssl-ocsp and transport-sctp. A production Vaadin application never runs it: Tomcat serves your requests, and netty is there because Copilot, a development mode tool, declares it. Nothing outside netty refers to the stomp, xml, redis, sctp or OCSP code at all. The rest runs only when your own code uses reactor-netty (WebClient, WebFlux), or on 24.9 and 24.10 when Control Center runs on Kubernetes, whose client reaches your API server through Vert.x on netty. Otherwise nothing calls it; if one applies, set the property below.
findings.fix_expected: Spring Boot decides this version, not Vaadin. No free Spring Boot release a Vaadin 24 line declares pins a fixed netty: 3.2.12, 3.4.13 and 3.5.16, the newest of their lines on 2026-10-24, pin 4.1.115.Final, 4.1.130.Final and 4.1.135.Final. It arrives when Spring Boot raises netty.version; until then, the property.
findings.impact: None for a production application without Control Center that makes no reactor-netty calls of its own. Otherwise the code handles traffic with the servers your own client calls, or with your Kubernetes API server.

findings.commentary: Vaadin does use jsoup, and each of these two needs something Vaadin does not do. CVE-2026-71497 is the Cleaner mis-parsing a malformed tag name that ends in a control character, and it bites only when the safelist you clean with permits a raw text element, which jsoup counts as iframe, noembed, noframes, script, style, textarea, title and xmp. Vaadin cleans with Safelist.none() in the action shortcut and the route not found page, with Safelist.relaxed() in the spreadsheet, the classic Panel and the appsec kit, and in the rich text editor with Safelist.basic() plus img, h1, h2, h3 and s. None of those permits any of the eight, and on these versions no Vaadin API accepts a safelist of yours, so the configuration the advisory describes cannot be reached through Vaadin at all. CVE-2026-75140 is the XML tree builder copying the inherited namespace map on every start element, so it needs you to be parsing XML with jsoup, and Vaadin parses HTML.
findings.impact: None through Vaadin. Two things are affected and both are your own code rather than ours, cleaning untrusted HTML with a safelist you built that permits a raw text element, and parsing untrusted XML with jsoup.

findings.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
findings.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.

findings.commentary: The version is your Spring Boot's: 3.5.16, the newest 3.5 release, pins jackson-core 2.21.4, and no Vaadin release moves it. On this series Flow does call Jackson's parser on every UI request, including on event data your browser chooses, but the vulnerable regular expression is not on that path: it runs only when Jackson converts a JSON string into a float, double, BigDecimal or Number, and Flow never does that with what the browser sends. Hilla endpoints and signals, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own and your own JSON endpoints do, which is why this stays a risk until your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson.
findings.fix_expected: A Spring Boot 3.5 release that pins Jackson 2.21.7. Maven Central has none as of 2026-11-02, and no Vaadin release moves this version.
findings.impact: None unless your application binds JSON from the browser to a float, double, BigDecimal or Number through Jackson: a Hilla endpoint or signal, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own, or your own REST controller. There, a crafted number sent as a string makes the request spend excessive CPU.

findings.commentary: The jar is in your application and the flawed code in it is not reached. CVE-2026-89425 is in UTF8DataInputJsonParser, which Jackson builds only for a java.io.DataInput source, and only bites while reporting an invalid token. On 24.9 and 24.10 Vaadin does give browser data to Jackson, for example the history state of every navigation, but as a String that elemental.json has already parsed and written back, so it is valid JSON and goes to a different parser. Nothing on the 24 series classpaths outside Jackson hands it a DataInput. Code of your own that calls createParser(DataInput) is outside this answer.
findings.impact: None through Vaadin or Spring on the 24 series. Your own code that parses a DataInput with Jackson is a separate question.
